conditions.unmeasured: figures downstream of a constant nobody has measured are absent rather than estimated
conditions.what_an_interval_here_is: a statement about this model's declared inputs, and nothing about whether the model has the right structure (ch14, ch19)

produced_by.sampler: sizing.mc — inverse transform, Iman-Conover rank correlation

correlations.because: As in the web service model (ch14): a busier service is usually a slower one per request, so the two rise together, and treating them as independent understates the tail.

summary.description: The web service's fleet as ch10 sizes it, with one change: some of last generation's hosts are still in service, doing the same job as the new ones. The question stops being how many hosts and becomes how many new hosts, given the old ones. The demand is the web service's own chain, copied node for node with the same ranges. How requests are spread decides whether the two generations' capacity adds. Data is placed by capacity in both cases; only the routing of requests changes.

annual_energy_cost.formula: (old_hosts * old_host_power + new_hosts * new_host_power) * pue * hours_per_year * electricity_price
annual_energy_cost.label: energy per year

provenance.source: ch04 — lognormal because growth compounds and the factor cannot be zero or less. One future in ten grows by less than 12% a year, and one in ten by more than 60%; outside that range you would be surprised. One factor for requests and for records, because users drive both.

busy_cores.label: cores busy at the busy hour
busy_cores.note: Arrival rate times service demand. It is a count of cores doing work, it has nothing to do with how many you own, and it is the numerator of every utilisation figure below.

ceiling.because: The web service's memory ceiling (ch08), on the pool as bought. Past the limit, memory cannot hold the whole working set and some reads go to disk, which the service time per request does not include. The old hosts carry more memory than the new, so this is the ceiling their retirement moves most.

provenance.source: the web service model's cache margin (ch08, ch11): room for the working set to grow before it spills out of memory
the web service model's host (ch10): spec sheet, physical cores

cores_per_old_host.label: cores per old host
cores_per_old_host.note: One number: the old hosts are already bought, and you can read their specification off the hosts themselves.

provenance.source: this worked example's premise: last generation's hosts have half the cores of this generation's. Fixed, because the hosts are already bought

ceiling.because: The web service's disk ceiling, on the pool as bought. A pool whose disks are full cannot take a dead host's records, and the margin is the same node the sizing used (ch11).

provenance.source: the web service model's disk margin (ch11): room to re-replicate a dead host's records onto the survivors
the web service model's host (ch10): spec sheet, one local drive

disk_per_old_host.label: disk per old host
disk_per_old_host.note: One number: the old hosts are already bought, and you can read their specification off the hosts themselves.

provenance.source: this worked example's premise: the same drive as the new hosts
Lognormal, the same range as the web service model's electricity price

ceiling.because: N+1 in a mixed pool means surviving the loss of the largest host, not an average one: that is the most capacity one fault can take away (ch11).

failure_headroom.label: utilisation with the host with the most cores down

provenance.source: the web service model's horizon (ch02): the refresh cycle the fleet is bought against
Lognormal, the same range as the web service model's host price

hot_fraction.label: share of records touched in a busy hour

provenance.source: ch08 — the working set as a share of everything held. Triangular; nobody measures this and everybody has an opinion, and the maximum is a service whose users all look at the same week's data
definition: 365.25 days of 24 hours
indexes, the write-ahead log and journals as a multiplier on stored bytes. Triangular, and the bounds are for a service with a few indexes per table — a search-heavy one is off the top of this range

largest_shard.label: one copy of one shard at the horizon
largest_shard.note: One copy of the stored data, with its indexes and after compression, split into equal shards. Real shards are rarely equal, so the largest is at least this big.

provenance.source: Lognormal, the same range as the web service model's licence per core. Charged on every core running, old or new

new_for_memory.label: new hosts the working set needs

new_for_requests.label: new hosts the requests need, routed by capacity

new_for_requests_equal.label: new hosts the requests need, routed equally

provenance.source: Triangular, the same range as the web service model's host power

new_hosts.label: new hosts to buy
new_hosts.note: The purchase, decided the usual way: the count the model recommends when requests are routed by capacity, at the point estimates. Held as an input, as the web service holds its fleet, so the ceilings can ask how the pool as bought fares.

provenance.source: the sizing decision: new_hosts_weighted at the point estimates (ch10, ch12)

new_hosts_equal.formula: max(new_for_memory, new_for_storage, min(old_short_equal + min(max(new_for_memory, new_for_storage) / one_host, 1), 1) * requests_with_new_equal)
new_hosts_equal.label: new hosts to buy, requests routed equally
new_hosts_equal.note: If memory or disk buys any new host, that host is in the pool and requests are held to the smallest host, even where the old hosts alone would have carried them.

new_hosts_weighted.label: new hosts to buy, requests routed by capacity

old_host_power.label: power per old host
old_host_power.note: One number: a premise of this worked example, not an estimate of any real host, so a range would be a claim nobody made.

provenance.source: this worked example's premise: an older host draws nearly as much as a new one for half the cores

old_hosts.label: old hosts still in service at the horizon
old_hosts.note: Not how many old hosts there are today: how many are still running at the horizon. Old hosts retire on their own schedule, and the check has to hold at the worst point, after they leave and before demand stops growing. Set it to nought to see that point.

provenance.source: this worked example's premise: thirty of last generation's hosts are kept in service to the horizon. A decision, because keeping them is a choice

old_in_service.label: any old hosts left
old_in_service.note: One while any old host is in service, nought once they have all gone. A generation with no hosts in the pool cannot be its smallest or its largest host. The new hosts are always there: *new hosts to buy* starts at two.

old_ram.label: memory the old hosts give the service

old_short_equal.label: the old hosts alone fall short, routed equally
old_short_equal.note: One if the old hosts on their own cannot carry the busy hour below the margin, nought if they can. The smallest host is a new one only once a new host is bought, so the question is asked of the old hosts alone first: old hosts with more cores than the new ones may need no new hosts at all.

old_support_per_host.label: support per old host per year
old_support_per_host.note: One number: a premise of this worked example, not an estimate of any real host, so a range would be a claim nobody made.

provenance.source: this worked example's premise: a maintenance contract on hosts whose purchase is long paid for. A share of a capital cost no longer counted would not describe it
definition

one_year.label: one year
one_year.note: An exponent is a count, not a length of time, so it has no unit. Dividing the horizon by one year gives the count of years, and `annual_growth` is applied once for each. Appendix D has the rest of the conversions that bite.

provenance.source: definition
Triangular, the same range as the web service model's os_reserve. The same share on both generations
ch04 — the busy hour, not the daily mean. Triangular, because this is an engineer's lowest, most likely and highest values; claiming more precision would be invention.

pool_ram.label: memory the pool gives the service

provenance.source: Triangular, the same range as the web service model's PUE

ceiling.because: The same ceiling for a router that sends every host the same share. The old hosts have fewer cores, so they are the busiest, and they reach the knee first while the new hosts have cores to spare. The pool bought for capacity-weighted routing is checked here too.

queueing_headroom_equal.label: the smallest host's utilisation, routed equally

ceiling.because: The web service's queueing ceiling (ch06), for a pool whose router sends each host requests in proportion to its cores. Then every host is equally busy and the pool's cores add up.

queueing_headroom_weighted.label: utilisation at the busy hour, routed by capacity

provenance.source: the web service model's queueing margin (ch06, ch11): how far under the knee the fleet runs at the busy hour

ram_for_service_new.label: memory the service can use, per new host

ram_for_service_old.label: memory the service can use, per old host

provenance.source: the web service model's host (ch10): spec sheet, the modules fitted

ram_per_old_host.label: memory per old host
ram_per_old_host.note: One number: the old hosts are already bought, and you can read their specification off the hosts themselves.

provenance.source: this worked example's premise: last generation's hosts were bought memory-heavy, with twice this generation's memory and half its cores

measured.corpus: bench.measure.application_records — JSON user profiles, orders and events in a 20/50/30 mixture, 128-bit identifiers, seeds 0-7

provenance.source: three copies of every record, so that a host can die and take its disks with it. A different durability scheme substitutes its own factor here and the rest of the model is unchanged, which is the point of it being a node

requests_with_new_equal.label: new hosts the requests need once any new host is in the pool, routed equally
requests_with_new_equal.note: Once one new host joins the pool, the smallest host is the smaller generation, and every host is held to its cores.

service_demand.label: CPU time per request
service_demand.note:
Core-seconds of work one request costs, which is not how long a request takes. A request that occupies one core for twelve milliseconds has a service demand of twelve milliseconds whether it returns in twelve milliseconds or in twelve seconds — the difference is queueing, and Part II is about that difference.
This is the model's one rate constant and it belongs on a rig (ch03). No rig is declared, so it is held here as an assumption whose source says what would replace it, rather than as a measured node with nothing behind it.

provenance.source: The lowest, likeliest and highest values are this book's own choice for the running example: not measured on any machine, not taken from any product. It is held as an assumption because no reference machine is declared in `rig/machine.yml`; `make measure-rig` on a declared machine replaces it with a measured one. It is triangular, with three values, because it has not been measured. Once it is, it becomes a normal spread around the measurement, which is a change of claim and not only of numbers (ch13).

ceiling.because: A shard has to fit on one host, and it can land on the smallest. The pool's total disk says nothing about that, so the smallest host sets the limit. The margin is the disk margin, because the host still has to take a dead host's records.

shard_fit.label: largest shard against the smallest host's disk

shards.label: shards the data is split into

provenance.source: this worked example's premise: the records are split into sixty-four shards, each held whole by one host and copied to others

stored_data_t0.label: records held, day one
stored_data_t0.note: This one keeps its single number. You can go and count how much you hold today. Nobody can count next quarter's busy hour. What is uncertain about the records is how fast they grow, and annual_growth carries that for the rate and the level alike.

provenance.source: The service owners estimate what the service holds today: its database and the objects users have uploaded, before replication, indexes or compression. It has not been counted yet, and counting it would turn the estimate into a fact.
Triangular, the same range as the web service model's support rate: a yearly share of the capital cost

utilisation_after_losing_largest.label: utilisation after losing the host with the most cores

utilisation_smallest_equal.label: the smallest host's utilisation, requests routed equally

scenario.because: Thirty of last generation's hosts stay in service to the horizon, and the new hosts are bought for what they cannot cover, with requests routed by capacity. Every figure the book quotes for this model comes from here unless it says otherwise.
